Messages.Author: Davey Hathorn
Messages.Body:
So, at the beginning of my turn, I control a Monocle of Clarity. I ask
my prey the following question:

"If one of my minions and one of your minions get into combat, will
combat end with one of them going into torpor?"

My prey, playing a combat-heavy deck, replies "Yes."

I then bleed him with a Outcast Mage. Now come the questions:
- If he blocks and we enter combat, must necessarily he choose a vampire
to block with instead of an ally? By his monocle answer, he *must* try
to send at least one minion of ours to torpor, and since only vampire
minions can go to torpor, does that mean he must block with a vampire
(or not at all?)

- If he blocks with a vampire and we enter comabt, must he do everything
he possibly can to send his *own* minion into torpor, since mine cannot
possibly go there? For instance, say the mage has 1 life left, and
moves to long range after playing a trap. At short range, he'll get
creamed by mere hand damage and combat will end with no one going to
torpor, so it seems like my prey must leave things at long range. Then
the mage strikes with 1R for a few round, while my prey's vamp goes
"wiff, ow." Furthermore, it would seem that my prey would be obligated
to play a non-destructive combat card in order to keep the trap going
(for instance, Wolf Claws or Undead Strength at long range) since he is
obligated to do all he can to send one of our minions to torpor.

- Suppose instead I had bled my prey with Rufina Soledad. He blocks
with a vampire. In the first round of combat, Rufina is pummeled by an
8 point strike! But then she plays basic Undead Persistence. She now
has no blood, and will not go into torpor until *after* combat, as long
as I keep playing cards. Is my prey obligated by the Monocle to send
his own vampire into torpor?

Are there any other suggestions of how to use the Monocle in a way that
makes it worth putting in a deck?

-davey!

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
Greetings. Please be warned that my answers to your questions represent
only my highly unofficial opinion about how this rarely played card should
be handled.

On Tue, 17 Nov 1998, Davey Hathorn wrote:

> So, at the beginning of my turn, I control a Monocle of Clarity. I ask
> my prey the following question:
>
> "If one of my minions and one of your minions get into combat, will
> combat end with one of them going into torpor?"
>
> My prey, playing a combat-heavy deck, replies "Yes."

OK. So far, I would say that we have a problem already. Card text
dictates that one must answer truthfully. "I don't know," seems to me to
be the only possible truthful answer here.

In fact, I would argue that "I don't know" is the only possible truthful
answer to any question about the future. It also resolves alot of the
headaches associated with the card.

If asked about one's current intentions, then I suppose one could legally
answer "yes". One would not be able to verify truthfulness in such a
case. There has never been a necessary connection between current
intentions and future actions. A person asked about future intentions
could well change his mind, and this would not prove that he lied. This
is the fault of the questioner for asking a question for which
truthfulness can never be enforced or verified.

The answerer would not be bound by his answer, as the question was not
framed as a question about the future. Thus, the relevant card text about
"abiding by the answer" in such cases would not apply.

Indeed, I feel it should never apply, as "I don't know" is not something
you can be forced to abide by, and I feel that should be the only possible
answer to genuine questions about the future.

[snip]

> Are there any other suggestions of how to use the Monocle in a way that
> makes it worth putting in a deck?

Yes.

Don't ask questions about the future.

Don't ask questions about intentions.

Ask verifiable questions about:
- Contents of Hand
- Contents of Uncontrolled Region.

Such as "Do you have a Majesty in your hand?"
or "Do you have any bleed actions or bleed modifiers in your hand?"
or "Is this (uncontrolled) vampire larger than 4 capacity?"
or "Do you have an Archon Investigation in your hand? ('cause I was
thinking of bleeding you for 6)"

Only ask questions where he cannot plausibly claim that he does not know
the answer.

As a final note...alot of people seem to assume that one must answer "Yes"
or "No". Nowhere does it say this. The only restriction on one's answer
is that it must be truthful.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Lupus Australis wrote:
> As a final note...alot of people seem to assume that one must answer "Yes"
> or "No". Nowhere does it say this. The only restriction on one's answer
> is that it must be truthful.

It says to ask a "yes or no question". Such a question, by definition,
requires a "yes" or a "no" as an answer. "I don't know" isn't an
answer to such a question - just an assertion that one doesn't know
the answer.

Questions about the future must be answered ("yes" or "no"), and
the answerer must abide by that answer *if possible*. (card text)

An assertion that one doesn't know the answer _is_ an answer. For example,
if I ask you, "Is my coffee mug at work a blue mug?" you must answer "I don't
know" because you don't. The question is certainly a "yes or no" question.

Besides, grammatical subtleties should be well outside the scope of the
rules team...unless, of course, they teach English for a living. And since
there is no errata to the contrary, "I don't know" should be a perfectly
acceptable answer when one doesn't know.

> the answerer must abide by that answer *if possible*. (card text)

A question about the future does not have to be answered "yes" or
"no" if one doesn't know. I would argue that a question about future
intent is valid, but a question about future results is not.

I think that we all can see why the Monocle of Clarity is banned from
tournament play.

or 'No', but they are then being forced to answer non-truthfully.

doesn't say that you don't have to answer truthfully, or that you can
answer something other than 'yes' or 'no'. It seems to me that allowing
"I don't know" answers would be a reasonable solution to the problem of
questions that you in fact do not know the answer to - which could include
all questions about the future, potentially.

I'd first like to say that I am not anything like an expert on Jyhad
rules, but as someone who just graduated with a BA in English, I'd like to
comment on the English portion of this, since much of this turns on the
English language and standard definitions of words and phrases.

A "yes or no question" is *NOT* a question that can only have two possible
answers. A "yes or no question" is one that can be answered yes or no.

For example:

"How old are you?" is not a yes or no question.

"Are you 50 years old?" is.

However, a person asked this could respond in many ways:
"yes," "no," "that's none of your business," or "Didn't your mother
teach you never to ask a lady her age or her weight?" :)

An example from real life: a British reporter was interviewing the
remaining members of the sex pistols about a new tour they were planning a
year or two ago. He asked several "yes or no" questions.

"Isn't it true that there won't be anybody under 40 at your concerts?"
"You talk about originality. Have you written any new songs for this
tour?"
"Isn't this a nostalgia tour?"

He was answered not with "yes" or "no" but with a chorus of obscenities
and several offers to kick his @$$. :)

For the record, a yes or no question doesn't put any "by definition"
restrictions on the answer a person gives. "I don't know" is an
acceptable answer (in real life - I'm not really talking about Jyhad
here), and the only truthful answer possible if one doesn't know.

restricts the answerer to only two possible answers, regardless of
knowledge, accuracy, truth, or whatever," but rather "a question that can
be answered with 'yes' or 'no.'" There is a difference.

On Wed, 18 Nov 1998, LSJ wrote:

> Lupus Australis wrote:
> > As a final note...alot of people seem to assume that one must answer "Yes"
> > or "No". Nowhere does it say this. The only restriction on one's answer
> > is that it must be truthful.
>
> It says to ask a "yes or no question". Such a question, by definition,
> requires a "yes" or a "no" as an answer.

OK, but that is not the phrase normally means. A "yes-or-no question" is
a type of question for which the answers "yes" or "no" would be meaningful
(though not necessarily accurate) answers.

For instance, "What color is her hair?" is not a yes/no question because
"yes" would not be a meaningful answer. If I ask "Is her hair brown?"
that *is* a yes/no question. But this does not mean the respondent must
answer yes or no. "Usually", "Sometimes", "Sort of", "Partially", and
"When she wants it to be" are all perfectly acceptable answers, and may in
fact be more accurate and informative than a plain "yes" or a plain "no".

The phrase is used in a number of games to limit the types of questions
that a questioner may ask, and not to limit the responses of the answerer.

For instance, if you have ever played with a "magic 8-ball" you know that
you are supposed to ask the 8-ball yes or no type questions. You also
know that the 8-ball almost never gives a simple "yes" or "no" as an
answer.

Similarly, in the game "20 questions", one person thinks of a person,
place or thing, and the second person asks a series of questions in order
to try to determine what the person is thinking of. The questioner is
limitted to "yes or no" type questions, because without this restriction,
he could simply ask "What are you thinking of?" and the game would
instantly be over. But the respondent is not limited to "yes" or "no" as
an answer. He is merely obliged to answer truthfully and without undue
evasion. Usually he will answer simply "yes" or "no" in order to give
away as little information as possible, but sometimes it might be more
honorable to say, for instace, "Sometimes" or "Partially", if either a
"yes" or a "no" would be too misleading.

> "I don't know" isn't an
> answer to such a question - just an assertion that one doesn't know
> the answer.

Techically, you may be right. "I don't know", is not phrased as an
answer. To phrase it as an answer, one should say something like "maybe"
or "possibly". But people usually say "I don't know," in order to clarify
that they are not being evasive, but are being as accurate as their
knowledge allows.

In "20 questions" it would be misleading and unsportsmanlike to answer
"yes" or "no" if you did not know the answer. In a court of law it might
be perjury.

> Questions about the future must be answered ("yes" or "no"),

OK, but that is not apparent from card text, and appears to be
contradicted by the requirement that one answer "truthfully".

I would argue that further errata is required to make this clear.

> and
> the answerer must abide by that answer *if possible*. (card text)

It is apparent from this clause that the card designers intended players
to be bound by answers about their intentions.

But this would only apply only if they chose to give any definite answers
about intentions. It is not clear from card text that they are obliged to
do this.

statement were a truthful answer, then you would know a truthful answer
because you'd know what your statement is. But your statement states
that you don't know any truthful answer. Logically therefore "I don't
know" can never be a truthful answer to the Monocle, because if it were
you would be giving an answer that says you have no answer to give,

let <foo> = "x=2"

pertain to future intentions, but also works in those rare times when
someone *does* know the future results.

On Thu, 19 Nov 1998, LSJ wrote:

> Lupus Australis <jbwh...@dorsai.org> wrote:
> > On Wed, 18 Nov 1998, LSJ wrote:
> > > Lupus Australis wrote:
> > > > As a final note...alot of people seem to assume that one must answer "Yes"
> > > > or "No". Nowhere does it say this. The only restriction on one's answer
> > > > is that it must be truthful.
> > >
> > > It says to ask a "yes or no question". Such a question, by definition,
> > > requires a "yes" or a "no" as an answer.

[snip]

You are consistently using a formula of traditional logic that admits to
only two truth values to any proposition (True and False). Now I agree
that this system is a highly useful one in many circumstances. The flaw
in this traditional logic system is that it assumes access to some sort of
omniscient source which can not only correctly and unambiguously interpret
any proposition, but also answer it with certainty.

In the real world, people do not operate according to this "two truth
value" system. Outside the halls of mathematics and hard science, it is
rather less useful because people are not omniscient and cannot access the
mind of God. In the real world, propositions have many possible truth
values: True, False, and various shades of Maybe (such as "probably",
"probably not", and "almost certainly"). Computer Programmers attempting
to simulate human intelligence have long recognized the limitations of
traditional logic for this purpose, hence the development of "Fuzzy
Logic."

Fuzzy Logic has of course existed long before computers. In a Court of
Law, if you are asked a yes/no question and are directed to "answer
truthfully", it is perfectly acceptable to give an indefinite answer such
as "Maybe", provided this is indeed a truthful answer and you are in fact
uncertain. Indeed, it would be untruthful and perjurous to do anything
else. Obviously the court accepts the existence of other truth values
besides True and False, since both values can be incorrect in some cases.

I recognize your position that "indefinite anwers" are not really
"answers" at all. But this narrow definition applies only within the
framework of traditional logic. It has very little to do with how the
word is generally used, or the "answers" that most people use to run their
lives.

> > For instance, "What color is her hair?" is not a yes/no question because
> > "yes" would not be a meaningful answer. If I ask "Is her hair brown?"
> > that *is* a yes/no question. But this does not mean the respondent must
> > answer yes or no.
>
> Right. Because the Monocle is not involved. If the question is asked
> via the Monocle, then the respondent must answer "yes" or "no" (actually,
> the question is not legal, since it doesn't pertain to the game).

> > "Usually", "Sometimes",
>
> The "is" in the question restricts the topic to the present.
> If "now" is part of the "usually" or "sometimes" that her hair
> is brown, then the answer is "yes". Otherwise, the answer is "no".

This is a good example of how the idealized concepts of traditional logic
presume omniscience, and have little relevance to most real-world
situations.

If you were to ask me, of a certain female, "Is she a brunette?", then the
chances are excellent that the female in question is not present, or that
if she is, that her hair is not visible to either of us. You knew that I
was not omniscient when you asked the question, and I know that you knew
this. Therefore, for me to place excessive emphasis on your use of the
present tense, and respond accordingly, would be disingenuous.

If I am honest, I know you know I am not omniscient, and that you are
requesting some sort of more-or-less indefinite answer based on degrees of
probability.

> > "Sort of", "Partially", and
>
> Both of these are either "yes" or "no" depending on the answerer's
> perception of what constitutes "hair being brown".

Right. Again, this is exactly the sort of ambiguity that makes
traditional two-truth-value logic useless in many real-world situations.

> > "When she wants it to be"
>
> Again either "yes" or "no" depending on what it "is" now.

See above.

> > are all perfectly acceptable answers, and may in
> > fact be more accurate and informative than a plain "yes" or a plain "no".
>
> Providing information as your reply doesn't change the fact
> that the answer to the question is either "yes" or "no".

This "fact" is a construct of traditional logic, and applies only within
its framework. Other frameworks exist, and could be applied.

> > The phrase is used in a number of games to limit the types of questions
> > that a questioner may ask, and not to limit the responses of the answerer.
>
> Right.
> But in this case, the card limits the responses of the answerer.
> "I don't want to answer", no matter how truthful a response, is not
> allowed by Monocle (nor by most of these "number of games").

I agree that "I don't want to answer" is not an acceptable answer. It is
not an answer at all, even within everyday or "Fuzzy" logic. A Court of
Law would not accept such as an answer, nor would a player of "20
questions", and it is not even included on most Magic 8-balls.

> > For instance, if you have ever played with a "magic 8-ball" you know that
> > you are supposed to ask the 8-ball yes or no type questions. You also
> > know that the 8-ball almost never gives a simple "yes" or "no" as an
> > answer.
>
> <groan>
> The 8-ball responds.
> And that response isn't restricted to being "truthful".
>
> The response-answer of the 8-ball is not the same as the correct-answer
> required by Monocle.

The point is that the answers given by the 8-ball are indeed "answers"
according to the everyday definition of the word -- according to the
"fuzzy logic" definition.

> > Similarly, in the game "20 questions", one person thinks of a person,
> > place or thing, and the second person asks a series of questions in order
> > to try to determine what the person is thinking of. The questioner is
> > limitted to "yes or no" type questions, because without this restriction,
> > he could simply ask "What are you thinking of?" and the game would
> > instantly be over. But the respondent is not limited to "yes" or "no" as
> > an answer.
>
> <groan>
> Maybe not where you play, but here the "thinker" must always respond
> with "yes" or "no".

Where I live, anyone who did not know the answer, but gave a definite
answer anyway, would be a cheat and a bad sport. I strongly suspect it
is exactly the same where you live.

For instance, suppose I am thinking of a lobster, and am asked "Does it
have an exoskeleton?". Would it be acceptable to say to say "no" and then
later claim that I did not know what an exoskeleton was and therfore had
to guess? Clearly an honest, but indefinite, answer would be far more
appropriate.

> > He is merely obliged to answer truthfully and without undue
> > evasion. Usually he will answer simply "yes" or "no" in order to give
> > away as little information as possible, but sometimes it might be more
> > honorable to say, for instace, "Sometimes" or "Partially", if either a
> > "yes" or a "no" would be too misleading.
>
> <irrelevant> - Here (20 questions) as with Monocle, it is up to the
> asker to make sure that his question, when answered truthfully with
> a "yes" or a "no" provides useful information. If a truthful answer
> of "yes" or "no" is misleading, then that is the questioner's
> fault/problem.

I'm not sure how this rule can be applied to "20 questions". The
questioner does not know what the object is he is asking about and has no
way of knowing if the "thinker" can answer a given question with
certainty, or if the question will be ambiguous with respect to that
object. I could argue this in detail, but would rather we drop the
subject.

Your principle can be applied more appropriately to the Monocle. The
questioner *does* have an idea what questions can be answered definitely,
and which cannot be. He knows that if he asks about the contents of a
person's hand, that person should be able to give a definite answer, and
cannot plausibly say "I don't know". He also should know that if he asks
questions about the future, an indefinite answer is the only kind that can
be truthfully given. It would seem to me that anyone asking questions
about the future deserves the useless response he would gets, if truthful
indefinite answers were allowed, as I feel they should be..

> > > "I don't know" isn't an
> > > answer to such a question - just an assertion that one doesn't know
> > > the answer.
> >
> > Techically, you may be right. "I don't know", is not phrased as an
> > answer. To phrase it as an answer, one should say something like "maybe"
> > or "possibly". But people usually say "I don't know," in order to clarify
> > that they are not being evasive, but are being as accurate as their
> > knowledge allows.
>
> Both these are also not the answer.
>
> "Maybe the answer is 'yes'"
> "Possbly the answer is 'yes'"
> "I don't know if the answer is 'yes'"
>
> are all responses that may well be accurate - but they are not the
> answer, by virtue of the fact that the answer is either "yes" or
> "no" and none of the responses in question are either.

All perfectly correct, but only within the idealized framework of
traditional logic. In the real world, as well as in alternate logic
systems, the word "answer" is not so narrowly defined.

This framework is never applied when real persons, lacking in perfect
omnicience, are required to give truthful answers to questions about which
they may not have adequate knowledge. That is the case in a Court of Law,
where people are required to "answer truthfully", just as they are by the
Monocle.

I have no trouble with your use of traditional logic, except that when
applied to Monocle it causes a host of confusing headaches. Logic Systems
are merely tools, which should only be applied in circumstances where
theyt are effective.

> > In "20 questions" it would be misleading and unsportsmanlike to answer
> > "yes" or "no" if you did not know the answer. In a court of law it might
> > be perjury.
>
> Fortunately, we're talking about the Monocle, where it is required
> by card text.

Card text requires that one "answer truthfully" questions about the

the exact wording that may be used to denote the options of "Yes", "No"
and the many shades of "Uncertain", and respondents are sometimes allowed
to clarify their base answer with additional information. Anything outside
this, such as "I don't want to answer." or "I hate your guts" or "I'm a
doctor, not a mathematician" are not answers and would not be accepted as
such, even if they are in fact truthful statements.

As an example, if asked in Court, "Is Jenny a brunette", and I say
"Usually", this might be accepted as an answer corresponding to "I don't
know" with an explanation as to why I do not know. (On the other hand,
the court might, and probably would, demand that I clarify my answer.)

> as the "real life", Law Court, and Fuzzy Logic cases do, then
> "I don't want to answer" or even "2+2=4" would be acceptable
> responses to any question posed.

Fuzzy Logic does *not* allow any response to be considered an "answer".
Nor does it give the truthful respondent the option of picking and
choosing the answer he wants to give. He must assign *the* correct truth
value if he is "answer truthfully".

Let me summarize again the absolute/traditional vs. the "fuzzy" approach.
I am going to slightly oversimplify the "fuzzy" perspective, but it will
still be adequate as far as it relates to Monocle.

In the absolute/traditional approach, all properly phrases propositions
are presumed to have one absolute correct answer. The proposition is
either True, or it is False, and there are only two possible truth values
to any proposition. These truth values are absolute, not relative, and
will not vary depending on the perspective of the person giving the
answer. Truth is not judged from the perspective of any one individual
but from the infallible perspective of some hypothetical know-it-all.
Under this perspective, a person can answer falsely, even if he is not
lying, because the truth of his statement is not being judged from his
POV.

[All yes/no questions are essentially propositions with question marks at
the end, with "yes" corresponding to True and "no" corresponding to
False.]

The second approach is more relative. Truthfulness is judged from the
perspective of the speaker, and not from that of the Hypothetical
Know-it-all. Once again, the respondent is required to assign a
Truth-Value to a proposition, but from his own perspective. He can assign
three possible Truth Values: He can say that he believes the proposition
to be certainly True (corresponding to "yes"); he can say he believes the
proposition to be certainly False (corresponding to "no"), or he can
indicate that he is somehow uncertain (corresponding to "I don't know").
These are considered to be three different "Truth Values" in this system.
Only one of them can be correct. If a person does not know the answer,
and he says "Yes" anyway, then he is considered to be lying, even if this
answer would be correct from another person's perspective or from that of
the hypothetical know-it-all. In the fuzzy logic system, truth is relative
to the perspective of the speaker and is judged accordingly.

Thus, there is no comparison between "I don't know" and "I don't want to
answer" in the "fuzzy" system. "I don't know" assigns a truth value to a
proposition. This is either THE CORRECT answer (from the answerer's
perspecive), in which case he is being honest, or it is NOT the correct
answer, in which case he is lying. If he is to answer truthfully, the
respondent does not have options as to how he will answer.

[Note that a particular "fuzzy" logic system can have as many categories
of "Truth Values" as you wish. The simple one given above has 3, which
would work fine as far as Monocle is concerned. Actually, one's level of
certainty can be conceived as a point on a continuum, and will fit within
whatever categories you artificially delineate. Many pollsters give you 5
options, such as Certainly, Probably, Can't Decide, Probably Not, and
Certainly Not. As another example, a programmer might design a "fuzzy
logic" system with 99 categories, with a Truth value of "1" corresponding
to "Absolutely certainly no", "99" corresponding to "Absolutely certainly
yes", "50" corresponding to total indecision, and a the rest of the values
corresponding to various levels of probability and uncertainty in between.
Your categories will work as long as a given perspective can be fit into
one and only one mutually exclusive category. But no matter how many
categories you use, the truthful respondent must assign his answer to the
correct category. He cannot choose his answer.]

[One can even have a 2 value "fuzzy" logic system, as when the Courts ask
Jurors to answer a proposition with "Guilty" or "Not Guilty". This works
because, in theory, no matter what you feel about the chances of that the
accused committed the crime, you should be able to fit this into one or
the other category. This is not the same as the 2 value system currently
being used on Monocle, which, in practice, asks one to choose between
"definitely yes" and "definitely no" when ones true feelings do not in
fact fit into either category.]

In any event, using a 3-value "fuzzy" approach that includes "I don't
know" as the middle option, does not, by any logic, force one to also
accept other truthful statements like "I don't want to answer" or "I am
not a walrus".

Limiting the Monocle's answers to "yes" or "no" would be fine if the
questioner were limited to asking questions that can in fact be truthfully
answered by either one or the other answer. This might be taken as part
of the restriction that the questioner is limited to a "yes or no
question". "Will you bleed me next turn?" can not be truthfully answered
by a "yes" or a "no", and might not be considered to be a proper yes/no
question for this reason.

Messages.Author: Lupus Australis
Messages.Body:
On Tue, 24 Nov 1998, Davey Hathorn wrote:
>
> > You made many
> > unsupportable statements about language and logic such as "Yes or no
> > questions require a yes or no answer by definition."
>
> Actually, that statement is quite supportable; in fact I believe you
> agreed with it, although you qualified it by adding "...Only in the
> context of Traditional Logic (TM)," or something like that. That's a
> good qualification to add, though, because that's the context that is
> used with the Monocle.

Well, I take it back.

As I have already argued, a "yes or no question" is a TYPE OF QUESTION,
and not a type of answer. It is the nature of the question, and not the
nature of the answer, that determine what sort of question it is.

Such questions may indeed require "yes" or "no" as an answer. This
depends on the situation, on the rules of the game you are playing, on the
particular logic system you are using, or on your definition of the word
"answer". So, while it may make sense to say that the Monocle requires
this type of question to be answered with a yes or a no, it is not
required by the *definition* of the phrase.

...at least not by the definition I am familiar with (and have already
given).

Of course you could invent a definition that differ somewhat from mine,
and would require such answers "by definition".

Yes or No Question: A question that is formulated in such a way as
to require either "yes" or "no" as an answer.

Problem is: according to this definition it is very questionable whether
"Will you bleed me next turn?" qualifies as a "yes or no question". I
would think it is more a "how the *&%$ should I know" question or a "it
depends on what cards I draw" question, since those are the answers that
would normally be required by a truthful response.

In the context of Monocle a "yes" answer to such a question translates as
"Yes, I definitely intend to attempt bleed you next turn if I possibly
can, regardless of what happens in the meantime."

A "no" answer corresponds, in practice, to "No, I definitely intend to NOT
bleed you next turn regardless of anything that up until that point."

These are two rather extreme options, and the respondent is forced to
choose between them rather than telling (what would normally be) the
truth, which in most cases is that he intends to base his decision on
cards and effects yet to be played.

Properly framed as a "yes or no question" (in this sense), a question
about intentions might be framed as follows:

"Do you intend to attempt to bleed me next turn [if at all possible
regardless of what happens in the game before you initiate the attempt?]"

Here, either a "yes" or a "no" will be suitable to cover all possible
intentions I may have, and allow me to answer truthfully with either one
or the other. Of course, a "no" answer will not be bind me to any course
of action.

You will probably argue, of course, that this makes no sense because
everyone would say "no", and the future clause would be rendered
completely impotent. Not entirely true. A person might well answer a
question with "yes" if you give him a motive to do so, as when making
deals. The "future clause" of monocle would then enforce those promises.
You could, for instance use it with Succubus Club to guarantee deals made
that same untap phase.

Another possibly appropriate type of future question might be one that
gives the person adequate information to make a definite decision as to
what he will do, by giving a complete hypothetical situation of the near
future. Here's an example:

"Suppose that I were "Effective Management" on my coming Master Phase,
and then, as my first minion action, have Smudge attempt to equip with an
Ivory Bow. Assuming no other effects have been played by any Methuselah,
do you intent to attempt to block with intercept?"

This is a reasonable question of intent. The respondent cannot reasonably
say "I don't know" or "It depends" because he has been given a COMPLETE
hypothetical portrait of the game state. He will be bound by the future
clause only if the hypothetical situation becomes a reality. If the
Effective Management were Sudden Reversed, then a different game state
would result, and the answer would no longer be binding.

Here's another possibility:

"Suppose that, after you answer this question, the next thing I do is play
a Malkavian Prank, and that no other cards or effects are played by any
Methuselah. Do you intend to hold out either 1 counter or 4 counters?"

Again, it might reasonably be argued that he cannot truthfully answer "I
don't know" or "It depends" because he has been given a full portrait of
the game state on which to base his decision.

Either a "yes" or "no" answer would be binding, provided things unfold
precisely in accordance with my hypothetical. This would give me 50%
chance of guessing what he is holding.

I makes sense to me that the "future clause" should apply only to
statements about the future only to the extent that they are statements
about intentions. You cannot "abide" by a prediction in any meaninful
sense. One only abides by intentions, or promises. There is no
contradiction in predicting that Clinton will win the election but that
you intend to vote against him, any more than there is a contradiction in
saying that Reagon won in 1976 but that you voted against him. One's
predictions are either right or wrong, as only time will tell, regardless
of whether you contribute to making the prediction come true.

The Monocle should not ask for predictions anyway, since these cannot be
truthfully answered "yes" or "no", and are therefore argueably not proper
"yes or no questions" in the above sense. The question brought up earlier
that went something like "If I bleed you this turn will one of our minions
enter torpor" is clearly asking for a prediction, and not a statement of
intent. The answer will be determined in part by factors clearly beyond
the respondents control. It is meaningless to require that the respondent
"abide" by such an answer.

> Here's yet another argument that "I don't know" doesn't work. Consider
> the following thought experiment: Suppose I ask a very complicated
> question, like some kind of riddle about the current game state, the
> answer to which can be deduced as a definite 'yes' or 'no' (after a
> nominal process of elimination) by observing game pieces that every
> Methuselah can see. Now, when I ask you this question, you don't
> currently know the answer, and you don't realize it's a solvable

If you have been paying attention to my previous posts, then you ought to

if possible. This applies even if he has to think about his answer, or
check his facts, before answering. Now obviously the game should not be

> at them, maybe you are too lazy to read their names. When the other
> Methuselahs cry foul play, just explain that you are an imperfect human,

Messages.Body:
On Tue, 24 Nov 1998, Davey Hathorn wrote:

> Lupus Australis wrote:

> > > The Monocle does presume that all questions have definite answers;
> >
> > Well, it is nice that the Monocle has so much faith in the existence of
> > the Almighty, but since he will not be present to provide us with these
> > definite answers,
>
> Well, I guess my play group is just smarter than yours :P
> Seriously though a Monocle question always has a definite answer if it
> pertains to the current game and doesn't ask questions about questions.

Seriously, though, you can't be serious.

Questions should indeed pertain to the current game, but this has nothing
to do with whether the respondent can reasonably be expected to "answer
truthfuly" with a "yes" or a "no".

The "questions about questions" is merely a particularly egregious example
of the wide range of nonsense that I feel should be not allowed. This was
a case where you ask your prey "Will your answer to my next question be
yes?" If he says "Yes" then you frame your next Monocle question in such
a manner that an answer of "Yes" will cause him maximum damage. If he
says "no" you alter the phrasing slightly so that a "No" answer will do
the exact same thing."

This was not fair of course. It comes from asking him to answer a
question that he cannot be reasonably be expected to answer with a "yes"
or a "no" based on his current information. The most truthful possible
answer would be "I don't know, it will depend on what question you ask."
He is expected to "truthfully" say yes or no when he has as yet no idea
what these answers will mean.

To properly phrase the question so as to be answerable with "yes" or "no"
by the respondent, you would have to ask: "Do you intend to answer my
next question with a 'yes' (regardless of what happens in the meantime or
what that question is)?" The respondent could then truthfully say "no"
without being bound by the answer. "No" does not mean "I intend to *not*
say yes to your next question", it merely means "I do not *intend* to say
yes to your next question." It is a negation of the proposition rather
than its inverse, and totally true, as his intentions will not be formed
until the next question is asked.

Another example of an abusive and inappropriate question was provided by
you yourself. It went "If one of my minions and one of your minions get
into combat, will combat end with one of them going into torpor?" Though
not as easy to abuse, this is wrong for the exact same reasons that the
"questions about questions" example is wrong.

To summarize your example somewhat, your plan was as follows: If your
prey says "no" then you bleed him with your vampires and not worry about
him blocking, on the grounds that the rules now compel him to do all he
can to keep you from going into torpor in such a case. If he says Yes,
you enter combat with an ally, obliging him to "abide" by his answer by
doing all he can to send himself into torpor, since he is the only minion
in the combat for which this is possible.

Other examples could be devised, but they all use a variation of the same
trick. You ask a question where the full meaning of the question has yet
to be determined (because it lies in the future) Then, once the answer is
obtained, you manipulate the meaning of the question so that the answer
will be damaging to the respondent. In the process, you force him to
prove his truthfullness by "abiding" by intentions he never posessed in
the first place.

> > I don't see how it does us any good.
>
> This does us good by insuring that answers other than affirmation or
> negation are unnecessary.

This can only be done by asking questions that can be truthfully answered
by affirmation or negation...by the person who has to answer, that is.
I'm sure the Passage of Time will prove that questions about the future
will indeed have yes or no answers, but Father Time is not the fellow who
is being asked to answer the question.

I would say that a good rule of thumb would be that a question is
appropriate only when a "no" answer is in fact a negation of a "yes"
answer, and not something else. Otherwise, it is arguably not a proper
"yes or no question" as a truthful answer will not necessarily correspond
to either answer. If "yes" means "I intend to do X," then "no" should
mean "I do not intend to do X", and not "I intend to not do X".
